newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss politician sees no need for Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: Swiss politician sees no need for Holocaust fund.

text.p: Christoph Blocher, a leading Swiss industrialist and populist politician, told 1,000 cheering people on Saturday that Switzerland should neither compensate nor apologise for any alleged wrongdoing in World War Two.

Blocher, a member of the Swiss parliament, told people at a Zurich hotel that Switzerland should stand up against "the excessive accusations from domestic and foreign circles and demands for money," according to Swiss News Agency SDA.
Blocher repeated the nation had no reason to apologise for business dealings with Nazi Germany and it was an admission of guilt to contribute to a fund for Holocaust survivors.

Swiss banks have been accused by Jewish groups of hoarding money left by Holocaust victims and three of the largest banks recently announced they were donating 100 million Swiss francs to start up a fund for survivors.
The decision to set up the fund was aimed at diffusing the controversy while helping to repair the Swiss banking industry's image, bruised by the affair.
The Swiss government has delayed a decision on joining the fund, but the cabinet agreed on Wednesday to administer the fund together with the World Jewish Restitution Organisation.

Underscoring his opposition against any federal money being used for a Holocaust memorial fund, Blocher said it amounted to a betrayal of the Swiss people if companies, banks or the federal government pays for, or apologises for Switzerland's economic policy during the war.

Similar statements by Blocher on Friday angered New York Republican Sen. Alfonse D'Amato, a harsh critic of Switzerland, who said it was shocking and appalling that an apology for collaborating with the Nazis was viewed as inappropriate.
But Swiss Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti joined a growing chorus of critics of D'Amato, saying the U.S. politician was neither interested in facts, nor a sensible dialogue.
"This man (D'Amato) is obviously neither interested in facts, nor in a sensible dialogue," Cotti said in an interview on Saturday with Swiss daily Tages-Anzeiger.
Cotti's criticism was directed towards a statement by D'Amato on Wednesday, in which he said the Swiss were viewed as guilty by the world and the debate was now about penalty.

Blick, Switzerland's largest daily, said D'Amato's criticism had gone far enough and it carried letters from readers saying D'Amato should look closer at how the U.S. treated its Native American population before he is too critical of other nations.

Cotti said it was not the first time that D'Amato had attacked the Swiss in an an insulting manner, but he was hopeful that people interested in cooperation would make sure that such such damaging attacks no longer took place in the future.

Noting that Blocher so far had shown great restraint in the debate of Switzerland's role in World War Two, Cotti said he was convinced the Swiss people supported the government and it was clear that no taxpayers money could be used for the fund.
Cotti said the government had not made any decisions or promises made about using federal money and a decision would first be taken when historians have laid out all facts.

The Swiss government is waiting to decide on joining the fund for results in the next few months from an independent study of central bank gold purchases from Nazi Germany and Berne's wartime policy of turning back Jewish refugees from the Holocaust.
"I am convinced the Swiss population supports this procedure," Cotti said.
Earlier this week Blocher raised the threat of a referendum if the federal government decides to contribute to the aid fund for impoverished Holocaust survivors.
Swiss banks have been accused by Jewish groups of hoarding accounts left by Holocaust victims.

The banks deny they deliberately kept heirs away from the money. But they agreed with the World Jewish Congress last May to a probe by an independent panel with unprecedented powers to lift bank secrecy in order to search historical records.
